message:
MESSAGE:
Hello. I make hand-poured candles at my kitchen table and I'm seriously thinking about whether to go full-time with it next year, after three years of doing it in evenings and weekends. I've got an appointment with the bank next week. A few questions.

Can you suggest a name for a new autumn scent that smells of apple and woodsmoke? And rewrite my product description opener so it's less generic: "This candle is a great candle for any room." Also, what's the difference between "gross" and "net" profit, in plain English? And recommend whether to sell at craft markets or on an online marketplace first.

Each candle sells for £28. Wax, wick, fragrance, jar and packaging cost me £11 per candle. How many candles do I need to sell each month to break even?

Could you give me three ideas for a launch post on social media? I'm pretty camera-shy so ideas that don't need my face would be ideal. Oh, and what label colour would suit an autumn range without looking like every other candle on the shelf? Everyone seems to use burnt orange and kraft paper at this time of year, and I'd love something that stands out a bit more on a crowded market table.

Thank you, any help with any of this is really appreciated!

RESPONSE:
# Name
**Windfall & Woodsmoke** is my pick. "Windfall" means apples fallen from the tree, and it also suggests a lucky find. Other options: *Orchard Embers*, *Bonfire Orchard*, *Smoked Cider*.

# Product description opener
Instead of "This candle is a great candle for any room":

> Bruised-sweet apples and curling woodsmoke, hand-poured at my kitchen table for the first properly cold evening of the year.

A shorter version: *"Orchard fruit meets bonfire night. Hand-poured, slow-burning, and made to make a room feel like autumn."*

# Gross vs net profit
- **Gross profit** is what you sell for minus the direct cost of making the product. For you, that's £28 − £11 = £17 per candle.
- **Net profit** is what's left after *all* your other costs too: stall fees, website or marketplace fees, insurance, equipment, travel, and so on. It should also cover a wage for you.

Gross profit tells you whether each candle makes money. Net profit tells you whether the business does.

# Craft markets or online first?
I'd start with **craft markets**:
- Scent is the main selling point, and people can't smell a listing online.
- You get instant feedback on scents, prices and packaging.
- You can build an email or social following from people who've already bought.
- It's good evidence for the bank that people will buy from you.

The downsides are stall fees and your time, so pick a few well-attended markets rather than many. Once you know your bestsellers, an online shop or marketplace can handle repeat customers. Note that with Christmas approaching, the next few weeks are prime market season.

# Break-even
Each candle leaves **£17** after materials (£28 − £11). Break-even is your monthly fixed costs divided by £17. I don't know your fixed costs, so here are some examples:

| Monthly fixed costs | Candles to break even |
|---|---|
| £800 | 48 |
| £1,500 | 89 |
| £2,000 | 118 |
| £2,500 | 148 |

Fixed costs should include stall fees, insurance, software, storage or workspace, and **a wage for yourself**. If you want to pay yourself £1,500 a month and have £500 of other costs, that's £2,000 ÷ £17, so about 118 candles. Also check whether market or platform fees should be added to the £11 per-candle cost, because they reduce the £17. The bank will likely ask for this calculation, so bring a version with your real numbers.

# Three faceless launch post ideas
1. **Hands-only pour video.** Show close-ups of wax being poured, the wick being trimmed, and the label going on, with a short caption about the scent.
2. **Still-life photo.** Style the candle with real apples, a bit of bark or kindling, and a just-blown-out match, with soft light. Caption it with the scent story.
3. **Name reveal.** Post a text-led graphic or carousel: "Which of these should I call it?" with 3 names, then announce the winner. It builds engagement without showing you.

# Label colour
Since everyone uses burnt orange and kraft, go dark with a small bright accent. Try **smoky charcoal or deep bottle green on off-white or black stock, with a pale apple-green or cream detail**. It suits the smoke-and-orchard theme and stands out on a table of warm oranges. A deep damson or plum would also work. Avoid kraft paper, as it's what makes you blend in.

Good luck with the bank next week!
